reviews.text: I'm not a big fan of survivor-likes, but I tried this one because it looked different. It's a lot of fun! Compared to Vampire Survivors, this game has a lot more going on moment-to-moment. The enemies throw projectiles, create damaging zones, and have other special attacks. The environments are highly interactive and highly deadly (avoid air conditioners). I love how you can combine weapons to make new weapons. In general, it's just a really fun and creative game. But it's hard too (in a good way). I'm 2 hours in and I haven't cleared the first area. The hip hop soundtrack is cool.

About a month ago, I fired up this relatively unknown game, Vampire Survivors. Apparently it caused a bit of stir when it was released a few years ago. I started it up and pretty quickly got trounced by some shuffling pixel ghouls, which stung a bit, since all I had to do was my little Belmont-like around and make some menu selections. I thought I'd give it one more go to see if I was missing something. 50 hours later, I can say I get it. When the new expansions, name change, and spin-offs were recently announced, I have to admit: I didn't feel much. I'm not saying I didn't have a great time, but I didn't feel the need to revisit the scientifically formulated way that game provided [i]enjoyment[/i] at the expense of [i]intentional engagement[/i]. In other words: I could turn my mind off and feel good, but I often felt just a little dirty after an extended play session. This isn't a judgement on the game! Or people's devotion to it! Just something I noticed about my gaming habits and what works for me. Beatdown City Survivors [i]is[/i] addresses my feelings in my (so far) brief one hour session since I picked it up yesterday for my Steam Deck. The systems are really engaging! For example, the environment plays a big part of what makes levels interesting, with several fluid systems (such as water, and, uh, sludge) that interact with each other, your body, enemy bodies, and other parts of the environment. Break open a fire hydrant and the water now covering the ground can carry the current from a downed power line. This can take out a whole group of enemies, but also [i]fry you[/i]. That same water can also wash the blood of the zombie hordes you've punched your way through so that your healing capacity isn't diminished. This kind of environmental awareness and interplay makes the game both fun and challenging! It also means player control is more sophisticated with dashes and the ability to instantly take direct control of the auto aiming of your attacks. This offers a level of expression that makes interacting with the apocalyptic nightmare of the city more predictable, offering you a ton of player expression. It's REALLY satisfying to pull off a butt-saving idea on the fly. Rescuing survivors adds a mechanical dimension to the game beyond just a new skin with a slightly different play style. They actually join you in your fight and need to be lightly managed as you make your way through the streets. They can really add to the carnage on screen, so you have a lot of incentive to rescue them despite the risk often being quite high to start. The presentation is spectacular, really. The sprites are detailed in both design and animation, reacting to attacks in ways that dismember and flatten, often while being affected by environmental effects. I laughed pretty hard the first time an army of mutated rats rushed me and ran through the flames of an exploded cop car. Their bodies were now burning, but were undeterred. I have played all of the Beatdown-verse games. I love NuChallenger's style, and their social and political commentary has only become sharper and more focused with each release. So far, I think its integration into every aspect of the game, from item descriptions, to the diegetic progression and level selection built into your home base, is the strongest yet. I mean, the setting, too, obviously. The music is on point. Love the grooves and the flows, and remind me of when I used to be in NYC on the regular. It absolutely fits the action and you should turn it up! The selections are thoughtful and speak to the holistic sense of place and culture that make you appreciate that indie game devs who create from what the know and love [i]outside of[/i] games make the [i]richest[/i] games. tl;dr: This is an action-packed, dynamic playground of a game that captures the love of a game developer has for their city, while critiquing the forces that prey on it. With excellent graphics and animation; a stellar hip-hop soundtrack, a high skill ceiling, and hilarious opportunities for player expression, Beatdown City Survivors takes what you already love and makes it something you can really sink your teeth into. ACAB.

I tend to play Survivor-likes while exercising in the morning. They don't require me to have any sort of twitch skill, but they're engaging enough that I forgot I'm exercising (very useful). This is my new favorite Survivor-like. It's got style for days through its incredible visual style and FANTASTIC soundtrack. The actual gameplay feels more dynamic than your typical survivor like, with hits having a bit more weight behind them, destructive environments, elemental effects, and objectives. Rescuing NPCs feels a bit like Dead Rising, but they often provide buffs alongside their combat support. NuChallenger have outdone themselves. A masterclass in the genre. I plan to play this for a very long time.

tl;dr—STRONGLY RECOMMEND—A fantastic new spin on a fun formula that absolutely stands out in this recently crowded genre. Disclaimer up front: I like NuChallenger! Backed Treachery in Beatdown City, and have been a fan ever since! I even try to chat whenever I’m lucky enough to bump into them at an event. But I didn’t get a free copy of this game and the rest of this review will be from the perspective of a Survivors-like enthusiast who’s put quite a bit of time into this game already. The first thing you notice when the game boots up is that Beatdown City Survivors is truly something special. You’re greeted with a killer track, slick pixel art, and the kind of satisfying sound design that can have you gleefully punching, kicking, and blasting your way through thousands of mutated monstrosities. And in this case, what you see is what you get—the whole time. Great music, huge cast of characters, plenty of things to achieve, unlock, and upgrade!! It’s clear that the developer was a fan of Survivors-type games AND also understood WHY THEY WERE FUN IN THE FIRST PLACE. The game plays about like you would expect! You choose a character, move them around an environment where nonstop hordes of enemies attack, collect orbs that eventually boost their level, choose either weapons or passive upgrades, and survive as long as you can. All while listening to fantastic underground hip-hop beats to survive to! Artists include Open Mike Eagle, SKECH185, Shrapknel, and more! Now for the twists! In addition to the common weapons you collect while leveling, each survivor has their own unique attack style and special move. For many these specials are just useful passive buffs, but for others, they’re actually powerful attacks! Weapons “evolve” on their own when you reach their final level and when you have two maxed weapons, you can combine them for fun, devastating attacks. You may have seen some of these elements in other Survivors games, but here they’re combined nicely. You’ve also got some environments to deal with! Sludge, poison, blood, water, ice, electricity, and FIRE! These can be a lot to handle, and they definitely provide a mix of fun and tension. Oh and stuff explodes! Yay! There are no randomized treasure chests to find (that I’ve seen—yet!) but you can unlock the ability to have a few random weapons appear on the battlefield. More importantly, Farooq will hook you up, assuming you have the cash! Mobile shops can be found all over the stages, and these can provide upgrades and crucial healing. They’re also a reliable place to combine/evolve weapons (rather than having to track down a random box). One last twist is the on-stage survivors that will actually team up with you after you’ve rescued them! You may not immediately unlock them as playable characters, but they will follow you around and help you survive! When you’re visiting Farooq, you can also choose to heal them or “extract them” safely (which may be a condition to unlocking them later). Once extracted, they will leave you (tragically) but they’ll also prompt Farooq to peel out and smash some foes with his glorious roach coach. Complete a stage by defeating its final boss (or die), and you can return to your base for upgrades or just to hang out and look at your achievements. If there’s one small gripe/suggestion I’ve got, it’s that I’m not inundated with dopamine after finishing a stage and seeing all my incredible unlocks and accomplishments. That said, it really is just a quick trip to the couch to see what you’ve done. Be sure to collect all your cash rewards so you can afford those beautiful, permanent upgrades. And don’t forget to head to the bedroom and see what characters you might have unlocked. Again, minor gripe! I wish there was more razzle and or dazzle when a character was unlocked. It took me a while to realize I was sitting on some fantastic, fun powerhouses! If you’re a fan of the genre, just get it. Now. Seriously. What are you waiting for?! You could be splodin’ monsters and listening to a kickass soundtrack RIGHT NOW! If you’re not sure or you’ve never played a game like this before, try the demo! Whatever you do, don’t just look at screenshots and go “nah.” I’m completely serious, here. I was NEVER a fan of twin-stick shooters or “endless horde type games” and then one day Vampire Survivors came around. A coworker recommended it, I went outside my comfort zone to try it, and it paid off big time. Just looking at pictures though, I can see why games like this might be ignored. It’s hard to really tell what makes them good until you FEEL IT. One final note for genre fans: This game really FEELS more engaging than some others—and I mean that in a good way. I always felt like Vampire Survivors rewarded a solid build and standing still (assuming you’ve finished collecting whatever you needed from the map). But Beatdown City Survivors definitely keeps you moving and reacting to hazards. In this way, I’d almost compare it to Megabonk (positively). Especially once you’ve unlocked the ability to upgrade the shop, hitting up as many Farooq-mobiles as you can will keep you surviving and thriving. And if you start to feel too comfortable, you may find yourself facing down an army of electrified gorilla zombies. Best of luck, survivor! PROS * Familiar, but with more than enough variety to justify the price of admission * Extremely fun and engaging * Great music * Delightful cast of characters, abilities, and fun weapon combinations * Absolutely accomplishes that “just one more run” effect CONS * Would like achievements and unlocks to be more “in your face” after a run * Could use more weapons Oh, and my true final ultimate last note: You may notice a shadowy figure in the character select/unlock screen. The description mentions they’ll be available in a future update. Hell yes. Updates incoming!!! \ ^_^ /

I have been having an absolute blast with the game so far. Pretty much been doing everything with only a few unlocks left. The style is fantastic, the music is great, and really I'm just having fun. The crafting system brings a little more variety to weapon combos that other games and leads to some really fun shenanigans, getting boot/chair, knife/board, bird/soda, and rocket chanclas leaves you an unkillable murder machine and it's just a delightfully mad silly time. I might be working on a longer review later but for now while it doesn't reinvent the survivor genre it's a damn damn good one of those

A Survivors game with a fresh take, solid challenge, and a killer soundtrack, this is a strong recommend for anyone that likes bullet hells or Survivors style games. There is a lot of depth in the game from weapon and passive combos, environmental hazards, and enemy variety. If you've played Treachery in Beatdown City, there are also a lot of well appreciated cameos and Easter eggs. Did I mention the soundtrack is great? Because the soundtrack is great. Definitely something you can pick up quick and unconsciously sink a few hours into.

Disclaimer: I'm friends with NuChallenger and have covered [url=https://medium.com/vidya-gaem-awards/the-v-gas-at-pax-west-2025-346cda4f2b2d]their game in the past[/url] on behalf of an outlet. Notwithstanding, I'll try and give it a fair assessment. Tl;dr, it's worth a buy. NuChallenger returns with Beatdown City Survivors, a follow up to their beat-em-up tactical RPG [i]Treachery in Beatdown City[/i]. That game had some hilarious dialogue and a long development cycle as things got to be right-sized. This time around, the focus is wholly on the gameplay, and it thrusts you right into the action with no tutorial apart from a few screens. The Survivor's-quality is largely in the horde enemies you have to dispatch which get progressively tougher and more numerous over time. But there's a dash mechanic, surface types and an environment mechanics which add a new layer of challenge. Much like that one Stamina mechanic everyone took from The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild for their own games, it's one thing to just copy, another to actually iterate - and luckily, they did it here. Of the roster, each character has a special ability, as well as strengths and weaknesses in their stats. A powerful character (Open Mike Eagle) can levitate and has a high debuff resistance but he also has low max HP, while some can double dash and attack faster but are weaker in their attacks. A unique quality about this game is its soundtrack, which is almost entirely comprised of licensed rap music. It captures the experience of playing a game late at night, with Spotify in the background very well. All in all, there are two full albums that play on shuffle ("Genuine Dexterity" by Kenny Segal & K-the-I???, and "Nobody Planning To Leave" by ShrapKnel") plus a few more individual tracks. These artists are also in the game as playable characters. But if the soundtrack isn't your thing, there's no gameplay impact by using your own music instead. Meta progression and modifiers, which are in the form of upgrades you can buy from Halal cart vendor Farooq back in the hub apartment as well as on the computer, help speed through future runs and get you closer to completing each level easier. Upgrading these were crucial to my progression, though part of me wanted to unlock the 1x continue easier. Probably the biggest surprise from the previews I played is that saving the fellow survivors isn't really a thing - some runs you might not even come across a survivor, saving yourself comes first. But that might be because they provide a buff on the battlefield and there aren't nearly as many that are as strong as you. Do I have any complaints? I have some. I think making someone complete the same map on a higher difficulty is just stretching playtime, but some people gave Kojima a pass for doing the same thing with MGSV when his team ran out of time. Additionally, forward progression (in the single-run, not metaprogression) can be lacking depending on the RNG due to the destructible objects not loading in a favorable spot. Some enemies also don't deal _any_ damage to certain characters at all (vs. deal major damage to other characters), and that wasn't something I was expecting. But, it's seriously fun and it puts a far more novel approach on the genre than I was expecting. Well done.

A good survival game, but definitely with some flaws. My biggest gripe: You barely notice yourself when you get damaged and how much. Sometimes I just glance somewhere for a second and suddenly I'm missing 60% of my health and I have no idea why. These sudden difficulty spikes really got on my nerves, especially early on. But I definitely like its style, setting, and how it feels to play. So consider this a very early review from someone, who will probably end up with a lot of time investing in this game.

I love this different take on the survivor genre. The music is a great vibe to this. There is a crazy amount of synergies available in the game to the point that I can still discover new ones while playing. There are unlocks that are both character specific and available to everyone. I've enjoyed my time with this game and I will come back from time to time to vibe and unlock everything.

A great twist on the Survivors-like Genre! Harder than many, the environmental hazards it adds keeps you on your toes, the weapons are varied and fun. and the rescued survivors add a nice little management aspect. The levels are fun and inventive, and it's very easy to get in the zone and beat up on zombies for an hour or two without noticing the time fly. The music selection absolutely owns, and adds to the immersion. If I was to add a major criticism, leveling and combining weapons is weirdly hard - I've had to wait until almost 18 minutes into a 20 minute level to finally get a combo before! Also, some combos feel like an outright downgrade, especially the ones that reduce range when you need to be kiting a boss. Anyway, definitely at least play the demo if you like survivors-likes and/or wish they were a bit harder. Bonus points if you love NYC and/or underground rap.

Yes, the soundtrack is great! It's refreshing to hear good rap in a game and in BCS the music not only sets the tone thematically but also syncs up with the rhythm of moving around the environments and kicking butt. This game feels a lot more frantic to me than other survivorlikes, which I appreciate, and a big part of that are the "living" stages filled with destructible objects and interactive elements, like oil that can catch fire from exploding cars, etc. The enemy mobs are also more dynamic and complex than usual and have personalities more akin to beat 'em up foes. They even fight each other and it's not uncommon to find yourself in situations where you're caught in the middle, trying to work around their behaviors as well as the stage hazards. If you feel like the survivor genre would benefit from some arcade energy, with big sprites, big freaks to fight, and fast, chaotic pacing right from the outset... then I think you should give Beatdown City Survivors a shot! It's the only game I know of where you can listen to rap music while you demolish giant rat men in a subway with a shiba inu and an army of pigeons carrying chanclas.

I'm obsessed with this game currently. The soundtrack and sound engineering alone is worth it-- I've been caught by my wife just listening to the menu, w/ its muffled 'from another car' effect on the music For the gameplay-- I've played a lot of different survivor-likes, and this is one of my favorites. The aesthetic is consistent, and hilariously accurate for NYC. The abilities on each of the survivors are varied enough that its easy to develop favorites, and they feel like playstyle preferences, rather than being super OP/etc. The only thing better than the weapons are the combined powered up versions. Where else am I combining tims and chancalas? Compared to other survivors, I found the balance interesting. Easier for me to unlock abilities and upgrades, but that didn't necessarily mean the entire game was much easier. The flow of a round is fairly consistent, although the different monsters/minibosses/bosses mean that each level feels different. My biggest critique is I want more levels; as it stands the game's got far fewer levels to look at than others in the genre, which makes a difference when you are repeatedly playing through each to unlock upgrades
